references.text: In the Song of Songs, the image of bridegroom and bride is used to describe the relationship between God and his people: "Go out, you daughters of Zion, and look upon King Solomon" (Song of Solomon 3:11). John the Baptist uses the same image when he calls Jesus the bridegroom.

The prophet Isaiah uses the image of a bridegroom rejoicing over his bride to describe God's joy over his people: "As a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you" (Isaiah 62:5). This is the background for John the Baptist's use of the bridegroom metaphor regarding Jesus.
Hosea prophesies that the Lord will betroth himself to his people in faithfulness: "I will betroth you to myself forever" (Hosea 2:19-20). Jesus as the bridegroom fulfills this promise.

Jesus refers to himself as the bridegroom: "Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them?" (Matthew 9:15). This confirms John the Baptist's testimony about Jesus as the bridegroom.
In the parable of the ten virgins, Jesus is the bridegroom who comes: "Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom" (Matthew 25:1).

Just before this verse, John the Baptist says that a person cannot receive anything unless it has been given them from heaven, and reminds us that he himself said: "I am not the Messiah, but I have been sent ahead of him" (John 3:27-28). The bridegroom image elaborates on this relationship between Jesus and his forerunner.
John the Baptist's conclusion follows immediately: "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30). The friend of the bridegroom finds his joy in serving the bridegroom, not in taking his place.
Paul uses the same bridegroom-bride image regarding Christ and the church: "I betrothed you to one husband so that I might present you as a pure virgin to Christ" (2 Corinthians 11:2).
Paul describes Christ as the bridegroom for the church: "Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her" (Ephesians 5:25-27). The bridegroom-bride image is central in New Testament theology.

In Revelation, the bridegroom image reaches its fulfillment: "Let us rejoice and exult and give him glory! For the time has come for the wedding of the Lamb" (Revelation 19:7). That wedding which John the Baptist pointed toward finds its final fulfillment.

Jesus speaks of perfect joy: "I have said these things to you so that my joy may be in you and your joy may be made complete" (John 15:11). John the Baptist says that his joy has been "made complete" (πεπλήρωται) by hearing the voice of the bridegroom.

Already in the prologue, John is presented as the one who was sent to testify about the light—not to be the light himself (John 1:6-8). As the friend of the bridegroom, his role is to point toward the bridegroom.
